sections.html:
Des Moines is Iowa's capital and the Polk County seat, built where the Des Moines and Raccoon Rivers meet. The part of the city south of County Line Road reaches into Warren County. The 2020 count was 214,133 residents in the city and 709,466 in the metro area, by a wide margin the biggest market in the state.

Sellers usually deal with a few distinct areas. Downtown and the East Village sit near the State Capitol on the east side of the Des Moines River. South of Grand is the older neighborhood around Salisbury House. Ringing the city are West Des Moines, Urbandale, Ankeny, Altoona, Clive, Johnston and Windsor Heights, and houses in those suburbs compete with city houses for the same buyers.

Most of the city belongs to the Des Moines Independent Community School District, the largest in Iowa, with East, Hoover, Lincoln, North and Roosevelt high schools plus an online campus. Small parts of Pleasant Hill and Windsor Heights fall in the district too. DART runs local, commuter and express buses.

sections.h2: Older houses and what buyers inspect
sections.html:
Des Moines began as Fort Des Moines in 1843 and became the capital in 1857, so many older streets date to the railroad and coal years. One block can hold houses from very different decades. Buyers of older houses usually ask for inspections of the plumbing, the wiring and the basement.

An owner who does not want to fund repairs before listing has another option, which is selling the house in its current condition. A cash buyer looks at the same plumbing, wiring and basement but prices what it finds instead of sending you a repair list.

Des Moines has flooded repeatedly, and buyers and lenders ask about it. A flood destroyed much of the early town in May 1851. The Great Flood of 1993 put the Des Moines Water Works under water on July 11. About 250,000 people had no running water for 12 days and no drinking water for 20.

A levee breached in June 2008. The Birdland neighborhood on the north side, along the Des Moines River, flooded in both 1993 and 2008. It now sits behind a rebuilt levee that cost $11 million, runs wider in many places and stands roughly 2 to 4 feet taller than the old one. Officials said tree growth had weakened the earlier levee and contributed to the 2008 failure, and that the new one does not remove flood risk.

  • Before choosing a closing date, find out from your insurance agent if the parcel is in a mapped flood zone.
  • Keep repair receipts and claim paperwork from past water damage, because buyers ask for them.
  • If the basement is damp, say so early. A cash buyer prices the condition in and does not need a repair list from you.

An owner who rents out a Des Moines house needs a rental certificate from the city. The Neighborhood Services Inspection Division inspects rentals and enforces the requirement when a house is rented without one.

The application asks that the owner's name match the Polk County Assessor's records. An owner who lives outside Polk County and its bordering counties must name an adult local management agent. The form is due back within 10 days, or the owner commits a municipal infraction, and a late form adds a $26 research fee.

The same division handles junk and debris, junk vehicles, illegal dumping, noise, graffiti and condemned buildings. It is at 602 Robert D. Ray Drive, 2nd floor. A vacant or inherited house that attracts complaints can pick up violations quickly.

  • Find the rental certificate if the house has been a rental.
  • Clear open code complaints, or tell a buyer about them in writing.
  • Check that the owner name on the deed matches the assessor record.

If the last day lands on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day. Late interest runs 1.5 percent per month, with a $1 minimum. A mailed payment counts as on time only with a postmark by the due date. You can also pay online at Iowa Tax and Tags. The Polk County Treasurer's office answers at 515-286-3060.

Unpaid taxes can be sold at the county's annual online tax sale, held each June. An owner who pays before the cutoff the day before the sale keeps the parcel off it.

At a sale, taxes are normally prorated. Either the buyer gets a credit for your share or you pay the treasurer directly at closing. Because Iowa taxes run a year behind, the September and March bills cover July 1 through June 30 of the prior year. Read the settlement statement closely.

On top of that comes the transfer tax, eighty cents for every $500 of value past the first $500, with a declaration of value filed alongside the recorded deed (Iowa Code 428A.1).

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work for a Des Moines house?
sections.html:
With no mortgage involved, a cash purchase has no lender appraisal and no loan approval holding it up. That can matter for houses with open permits, old systems or deferred repairs, which lenders sometimes will not approve.

  1. We ask about the condition, any liens and your timeline.
  2. You receive a written offer that you can accept or turn down.
  3. Say yes, and a title company takes over the paperwork while taxes are settled at the closing table.
  4. The closing date is yours to choose, as long as the title work is done by then.

If the house is an inherited Des Moines property, a rental with tenants or a home behind on payments, tell us up front. Those situations change the paperwork, not the basic steps.

sections.h2: What to bring to the first conversation
sections.html:
You do not need a perfect file, but a few items save time. Bring the address and a rough account of what is wrong with the house. Add the latest tax statement, any rental certificate, notes from past flood or water repairs and the names that appear on the deed. If a lien, a payoff or a code notice is open, say so now so the title company can plan for it.

Then compare. A cash offer is one price for the house as it stands. A listing adds repair costs, showings, inspection credits and the time a buyer's loan takes. Put both on paper and choose the one that fits your date and your budget.

sections.h2: Selling a Des Moines rental or inherited house
sections.html:
Rentals and inherited houses are common reasons for a quick sale in Des Moines, and each has its own checklist. For a rental, find the city certificate, the current lease and any notice from the Neighborhood Services Inspection Division. Decide whether the tenant stays or leaves, and write the date down.

For an inherited house, make sure the deed names match the people who will sign. A house that sat empty may have attracted complaints about debris or a vehicle, so drive by and clear anything that could draw a notice before a buyer visits.

faqs.q: What counties does Des Moines sit in?
faqs.a: Des Moines is the seat of Polk County, and the part of the city south of County Line Road extends into Warren County. The Polk County Treasurer bills property tax for most Des Moines houses.

faqs.q: Does a Des Moines landlord need a rental certificate?
faqs.a: Yes. The city requires one, and its Neighborhood Services Inspection Division enforces the rule. The owner of record must return the application within 10 days or face a municipal infraction.

faqs.q: When are Polk County property taxes delinquent?
faqs.a: The first half is delinquent after September 30 and the second half after March 31. After that, interest accrues at 1.5 percent a month, with a $1 minimum.

Some do. Low areas near the Des Moines and Raccoon Rivers flooded in 1851, 1993 and 2008, and the Birdland neighborhood on the north side now sits behind a rebuilt levee. Ask your insurer about your parcel.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Des Moines house with code violations?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can take the house as it stands. Open violations and liens are cleared by the title company at closing or dealt with in the contract.
